To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the performance of packet classification algorithms depends strongly on the rule set and that the memory consumption of a rule set can be predicted by its rule set characteristics.

the choice of a packet classification algorithm for a given rule set can be crucial to the performance of the system and that our Smart Split and Auto PC algorithms can be used to choose a packet classification algorithm that is suited to a given rule set.

(1) a same rule set induces different performance behaviour with various packet classification algorithms; (2) the performance behaviour is related to the intrinsic characteristics of the rule set; and (3) by using the characteristics of a rule set, a packet classification algorithm can be selected to yield optimal performance.
In summary, our research is concerned with

understanding the performance behaviour of various packet classification algorithms and rule set characteristics, as well as developing a framework that is capable of automatically configuring a multi component system for optimal performance.
the design and implementation of a meta-algorithm for software based packet classification.

the design and implementation of meta algorithms that are capable of automatically configuring a multi component classification engine for large rule sets, with the objective of minimizing the memory footprint, and maximizing classification performance.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the Smart Split algorithm and Auto PC framework provide a meta level packet classification solution that can automatically configure a multi component packet classifier for any large packet classification problem, and that outperforms any existing packet classification algorithms.

the Auto PC framework is capable of configuring a packet classification system with up to 20 times less memory consumption than the state of the art work [20], while obtaining up to about 6x faster classification speed.
our work is a major step forward in understanding the performance of packet classification algorithms.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we are able to automatically configure a packet classification system that is capable of achieving the best performance, in term of both memory consumption and classification speed, for a given rule set, by selecting the most appropriate packet classification algorithm and splitting a large rule sets in several subsets if needed.
we have identified and exploited the intrinsic characteristics of packet classification rule sets to achieve better performance.

we have proposed a meta algorithm for packet classification that automatically configures a multi component system to obtain the best trade-off between classification speed and memory consumption for a given rule set.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the performance of a given rule set can be predicted by the characteristics of that rule set.
a single packet classification algorithm is unlikely to be suitable for all rule sets.

a same rule sets can induce different memory consumption and classification speed for various packet classification algorithms, and we are able to model the memory consumption and identify a good packet classification algorithm for a given rule set.
